newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Japan business urges Vietnam to help investors.
newsitem.headline: Japan business urges Vietnam to help investors.

text.p: A delegation of Japanese business leaders has urged Vietnam to improve its foreign investment environment with a warning that overseas businesses could look elsewhere.

Akira Nishio, chairman of the Japan-Vietnam Economic Committee, told a news conference in Hanoi on Wednesday that the communist-run country faced risks as an investment destination from growing competition elsewhere in Southeast Asia.
"We told the Vietnamese that a country cannot choose the company, but the company can choose the country," he said.
Mishio's comments follow several days of meetings with officials from Vietnam's Ministry of Planning and Investment and senior leaders including Communist Party chief Do Muoi.

He and other members of the Japanese delegation shied away from outright criticism of Hanoi's investment policies, but said they had urged Vietnam to compete for overseas investment with other Southeast Asian nations.
"Vietnam should offer better, more attractive conditions," he said. "For example taxes, air fares, hotel and telephone charges are unreasonable and should be changed."
Nishio added both Vietnamese and foreign businesses needed clearer rules on borrowing money and said clarification was needed from the government on the country's industrial policy.
"I do hope they listened carefully because we emphasised with a loud voice," he said.

Japan is currently the second biggest investor in Vietnam after Taiwan, and its businesses have pledged some $2.4 billion towards 155 projects in the country since economic reforms were launched in the late 1980s.

But Vietnam's state media reported in September that Japanese investment pledges in the first eight months of this year had slipped to $335 million compared with more than $800 million in the same period a year earlier.
Nishio said he did not see the fall as an indication of declining Japanese interest. He said the year-end picture was likely to be more positive.

Vietnam's formerly glowing image as a new investment frontier has been dented over the last year by a series of high profile business failures and growing complaints from foreign investors over problems from heavy-handed bureaucracy to corruption.

Vietnamese officials say they recognise many of the problems and hope to address some of them with a new foreign investment law, which is expected to go before the country's National Assembly later this month.
